items.title: Nature of Indian Federalism, Territory & Reorganisation (Art 1-4)
items.body:
## Union of States

- **Article 1** declares India, that is Bharat, a **Union of States** — the term (per Ambedkar) signifies the federation is **not based on an agreement** and **no state may secede**: an *indestructible union of destructible states*.
- Indian federalism is **'federal in form but unitary in spirit'** (K. C. Wheare called it **quasi-federal**): a strong Centre, single citizenship, single integrated judiciary, all-India services, single constitution and emergency provisions all tilt power to the Union.

## Reorganisation of States (Art 2-4)

| Article | Content |
|---|---|
| 2 | Admission / establishment of **new states** into the Union (e.g. Sikkim, 1975) |
| 3 | Formation of new states, alteration of areas/boundaries/names from existing territory |
| 4 | Such laws are **not** amendments under Art 368; pass by **simple majority** |

- An Art 3 bill needs **prior recommendation of the President**; the affected state legislature must be **consulted but its view is not binding**.
- Landmark reorganisations: Andhra (1953, first linguistic state after Potti Sriramulu's death), States Reorganisation Act **1956** (14 states + 6 UTs), Telangana (2014), J&K & Ladakh UTs (2019).
keyPoints: Article 1 calls India a 'Union of States' — an indestructible union with no right of secession.
Indian federalism is quasi-federal: federal in form, unitary in spirit (strong Centre, single citizenship).
Art 2 = admission of new states; Art 3 = internal reorganisation from existing territory.
Art 3 bill needs prior presidential recommendation; state legislature is consulted but not bound.
Art 4 makes reorganisation laws non-amendments, passed by simple majority.
States Reorganisation Act 1956 created 14 states and 6 UTs on linguistic lines.
items.mnemonic: Articles 1-4 order: '1 defines, 2 admits, 3 alters, 4 clarifies (not an amendment).'
items.source: Constitution of India, Articles 1-4; APPSC GK PDF — Union and its Territory

items.title: Legislative Relations & the Seventh Schedule
items.body:
## Distribution of subjects

- Territorial extent: Parliament can legislate for the whole/part of India; a state legislature for its territory (**Art 245**).
- The **Seventh Schedule** divides subjects into three lists:

| List | Original / present subjects | Who legislates |
|---|---|---|
| Union | 97 → **100** | Parliament |
| State | 66 → **61** | State legislature |
| Concurrent | 47 → **52** | Both (Union prevails) |

- **Residuary powers** (Art 248) — including residuary taxation — rest with **Parliament**, borrowed from Canada.

## Parliament legislating on the State List

| Article | When Parliament may legislate on State List |
|---|---|
| 249 | Rajya Sabha passes a 2/3 resolution in the national interest |
| 250 | A National Emergency is in operation |
| 252 | Two or more states request it |
| 253 | To implement an international treaty/agreement |
| 356 | During President's Rule in a state |

## Repugnancy

- **Art 254**: on a Concurrent subject, a **Union law prevails** over a repugnant state law; exception — a state law reserved for and receiving **presidential assent** prevails in that state (Parliament may still override it).
keyPoints: Seventh Schedule: Union List (100), State List (61), Concurrent List (52) subjects.
Residuary powers of legislation and taxation vest in Parliament under Article 248.
Parliament can legislate on State List via Articles 249, 250, 252, 253 and during Art 356.
Article 254: Union law prevails over a repugnant state law on Concurrent subjects.
A repugnant state law with presidential assent prevails in that state, subject to parliamentary override.
items.mnemonic: State-List override Articles '249-250-252-253' = interest, emergency, request, treaty.
items.source: Constitution of India, Articles 245-255 & Seventh Schedule

items.title: Administrative Relations & Coordination Machinery
items.body:
## Union directions to states (Art 256-263)

- **Art 256** — states must ensure compliance with Union laws.
- **Art 257** — state executive power must not impede Union executive power; the Union may direct states on **communications and railways of national importance**.
- **All-India Services** (IAS, IPS, IFoS) under **Art 312** serve both the Union and states — a strong unifying, centralising device (RS resolution needed to create new AIS).

## Coordination bodies

- **Inter-State Council (Art 263)** — a recommendatory body set up in **1990** on the **Sarkaria Commission's** advice; chaired by the PM with CMs and select Union ministers.
- **Zonal Councils** — **statutory** bodies under the States Reorganisation Act 1956 (five zones + the North-Eastern Council), for inter-state cooperation.
- **Art 261** — full faith and credit to public acts, records and judicial proceedings across states.
keyPoints: Art 256-257: states must comply with Union laws and not impede Union executive power.
Art 257 lets the Union direct states on communications/railways of national importance.
All-India Services (Art 312) are common to Union and states — a centralising feature.
Inter-State Council (Art 263) set up in 1990 on Sarkaria's recommendation; PM-chaired, recommendatory.
Zonal Councils are statutory bodies under the States Reorganisation Act 1956.
items.source: Constitution of India, Articles 256-263 & 312; Sarkaria Commission Report

items.title: Financial Relations, Finance Commission & GST Council
items.body:
## Distribution of finances (Art 268-293)

- Taxes are distributed between the Union and states; **income tax excludes agricultural income** (a State subject).
- **Grants-in-aid**: statutory grants under **Art 275** (on Finance Commission advice) and discretionary grants under **Art 282**.

## Finance Commission (Art 280)

- A **quasi-judicial constitutional body** constituted by the President **every fifth year**, with a **chairman + 4 members**.
- Recommends: (i) **vertical** distribution of the divisible tax pool between Centre and states, (ii) **horizontal** distribution among states, (iii) grants-in-aid principles, and (iv) measures to augment state consolidated funds for panchayats/municipalities.

| FC | Chairman | Award period |
|---|---|---|
| 14th | Y. V. Reddy | 2015-20 |
| 15th | N. K. Singh | 2020-26 |
| **16th** | **Arvind Panagariya** | **2026-31** |

- The **16th Finance Commission** (constituted Dec 2023) is chaired by **Arvind Panagariya**; its award covers **1 April 2026 to 31 March 2031** *(verified online, Sep 2026)*.

## GST Council (Art 279A)

- Added by the **101st Amendment Act, 2016**; chaired by the **Union Finance Minister**, with state FMs as members.
- Centre holds **1/3** of votes, states **2/3**; decisions need a **3/4 majority** — a model of **cooperative fiscal federalism / 'pooled sovereignty'**.
keyPoints: Finance Commission is constituted under Article 280 every 5 years — chairman + 4 members.
Statutory grants-in-aid = Art 275; discretionary grants = Art 282.
16th Finance Commission: chair Arvind Panagariya, award period 2026-31 (constituted Dec 2023).
15th FC was chaired by N. K. Singh (2020-26); 14th by Y. V. Reddy (2015-20).
GST Council (Art 279A, 101st Amendment 2016): Centre 1/3 votes, states 2/3, decisions need 3/4 majority.
Union taxes income excluding agricultural income, which is a State List subject.
items.source: Constitution of India, Articles 268-293, 279A, 280; Ministry of Finance / PIB (verified Sep 2026)

items.title: Commissions on Centre-State Relations & Dispute Machinery
items.body:
## Commissions & committees

| Body | Year | Set up by | Focus |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Rajamannar Committee** | 1969 | Tamil Nadu govt | State autonomy; less central control |
| **Sarkaria Commission** | 1983-88 | Centre (R. S. Sarkaria) | Centre-State relations |
| **Punchhi Commission** | 2007-10 | Centre (M. M. Punchhi) | Centre-State relations (post-liberalisation) |

- **Common recommendations**: sparing, well-justified use of **Article 356**; a **consultative role for states** in Governor appointments; strengthening the **Inter-State Council**; the Governor should be a detached, apolitical figure. Sarkaria opposed abolishing Art 356 but wanted it a 'last resort'; Punchhi suggested a fixed **five-year Governor tenure** and 'localising emergencies' to troubled districts.

## Dispute machinery

- **President's Rule (Art 356)** was frequently misused until **S. R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994)** made the proclamation **judicially reviewable** and mandated a **floor test** to prove majority; it also affirmed secularism and federalism as basic features.
- **Inter-state water disputes** — **Art 262** lets Parliament provide for adjudication (tribunals) and **bar the jurisdiction of all courts**, including the Supreme Court; the **Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956** and **River Boards Act, 1956** operationalise it.
keyPoints: Rajamannar Committee (1969, Tamil Nadu) championed state autonomy and less central control.
Sarkaria Commission (1983-88) and Punchhi Commission (2007-10) reviewed Centre-State relations.
Common recommendation: use Article 356 as a last resort and consult states on Governor appointments.
S. R. Bommai (1994): Art 356 proclamation is judicially reviewable; majority tested on the floor of the House.
Article 262 lets Parliament set up water-dispute tribunals and exclude court jurisdiction.
Inter-State River Water Disputes Act and River Boards Act were both enacted in 1956.
items.source: Sarkaria & Punchhi Commission Reports; Rajamannar Committee Report; S. R. Bommai (1994)

items.title: Union Territories & Trends in Federalism
items.body:
## Union Territories (Art 239-241)

- UTs are administered by the **President through administrators** (Art 239), titled **Lieutenant Governor** or **Administrator**.
- **Puducherry** and the **NCT of Delhi** have **legislative assemblies** and councils of ministers with limited powers.
- The **69th Amendment Act, 1991** gave Delhi its special **NCT** status; **land, police and public order** stay with the Centre through the Lieutenant Governor, producing recurring Centre-Delhi friction that the Supreme Court has repeatedly adjudicated.

## Cooperative & competitive federalism

- **Cooperative federalism** — Centre and states work together: **GST Council**, **Inter-State Council**, **NITI Aayog** (replaced the Planning Commission in 2015, a platform for shared policymaking).
- **Competitive federalism** — states compete on outcomes/rankings (Ease of Doing Business, Aspirational Districts) to attract investment.
- Post-1991 liberalisation increased states' economic role, deepening both trends.
keyPoints: UTs are administered by the President through administrators/Lieutenant Governors (Art 239).
Puducherry and NCT Delhi have legislative assemblies with limited powers.
69th Amendment (1991) gave Delhi NCT status; land, police, public order remain with the Centre.
Cooperative federalism institutions: GST Council, Inter-State Council, NITI Aayog (2015).
Competitive federalism: states compete via rankings like Ease of Doing Business and Aspirational Districts.
items.source: Constitution of India, Articles 239-241; APPSC GK PDF — Union and its Territory; NITI Aayog

items.title: Fifth/Sixth Schedules & Extra-constitutional Bodies
items.body:
**Fifth Schedule:** provides for administration of **Scheduled Areas** and protects **tribal land from transfer to non-tribals**.

**Sixth Schedule:** provides **autonomous district/regional councils** for the tribal areas of **Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram**. Both schedules protect Scheduled Tribes.

**Extra-constitutional bodies:** the **Planning Commission** and the **National Development Council (NDC)** were **not mentioned in the Constitution** and were non-statutory; **Zonal Councils** are **statutory** (States Reorganisation Act 1956), not constitutional.
keyPoints: Fifth Schedule administers Scheduled Areas and bars transfer of tribal land to non-tribals.
Sixth Schedule gives autonomous councils to tribal areas of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram.
The Planning Commission and NDC were extra-constitutional and non-statutory; Zonal Councils are statutory, not constitutional.
